topic.name: Prompting for learning
topic.description: Write prompts that make AI act as a tutor or sparring partner — explanations at a chosen level, Socratic questions, worked examples followed by practice, counter-arguments, or feedback against criteria — rather than producing finished text, and judge whether the interaction produced learning. Effective prompting includes giving context and constraints, iterating, and stopping to work without the tool.
masteryEvidence: Writes prompts that specify role, level, task and constraints, such as asking to be questioned rather than given the answer
Uses AI to generate self-test questions or counter-arguments and answers them without assistance
Iterates a prompt when the output is too generic, too advanced or off-task
Judges whether an interaction increased their understanding by explaining the idea afterwards without the tool
Keeps prompting within the uses permitted for the task
topic.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write two prompts for preparing a seminar on an assigned reading: one that would help them learn and one that would replace their thinking. Check the contrast (questioning, explanation and self-testing versus summary or answer generation) and whether the learning prompt includes constraints and a follow-up step done without the tool.

guidance.summary: Kasneci et al. (2023) and UNESCO (2023) both stress that the educational value of generative AI depends on use that supports learners' own thinking rather than substituting for it. Self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002) offers a frame: prompting for learning means setting a goal, monitoring understanding during the interaction and evaluating afterwards without the tool. Teaching should contrast learning-oriented and output-oriented prompts and build in unassisted checks.

activities.title: Two prompts, two outcomes
learnerActions: Write an output prompt and a learning prompt for the same task
Run both and compare what they would learn from each
Explain the concept afterwards without the tool
activities.intendedInsight: The same tool can replace or support thinking depending on the prompt.
activities.rationale: Contrast makes the difference concrete; the unassisted explanation tests learning.

activities.title: Sparring partner
learnerActions: Ask a tool to question them Socratically on a reading
Answer without looking at the text
Ask for counter-arguments to their position
Write a short reflection on what they learned
activities.intendedInsight: AI can provide questioning and challenge that support understanding.
activities.rationale: Questioning and retrieval support learning; the reflection supports self-evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Prompts that ask for answers or finished text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot explain content they 'studied' with AI.
difficulties.response: Teach learning-oriented prompt patterns and unassisted checks.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting a too-advanced or generic explanation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report confusion but do not iterate.
difficulties.response: Model iteration: specifying level, examples and the learner's current understanding.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a prompt to help them understand a difficult concept from a lecture.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specifies level, asks for explanation and questions, and includes a self-test.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Asks for an explanation without constraints or a follow-up.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Asks for a summary or answer to submit.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: structured prompt patterns linked to course content. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific learning uses within module rules. PGR: using AI to test arguments and explore unfamiliar fields.
reviewNotes: Evidence on learning outcomes from AI-supported study is emerging and mixed; activities are proposals.
